lessons.title: Single-Threaded Constraints & Non-Blocking I/O
lessons.description: JavaScript runs on one thread — asynchronous code keeps the UI responsive while waiting for slow operations.

sections.heading: Single-threaded by design
paragraphs: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time on a single thread. If a slow operation blocks the thread, the entire page freezes. Asynchronous code solves this by letting the engine handle other work while waiting.
list: The main thread runs your code one line at a time
Blocking operations (network, file I/O) would freeze the UI
Asynchronous callbacks let the thread continue working
The browser handles async operations in the background

codeExamples.heading: Synchronous vs asynchronous behavior
explanation: Synchronous code runs in order and blocks the thread until complete.
setTimeout is asynchronous — it schedules a callback and moves on.
The main thread continues to console.log("3") without waiting.
The callback runs later when the timer expires and the thread is free.

practice.task: Write code that logs 1, then schedules a setTimeout for 2 seconds that logs 2, then logs 3. Predict the output order before running.
hints: setTimeout is asynchronous — it runs after the synchronous code finishes.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript is single-threaded — it runs one piece of code at a time.
Asynchronous code lets the thread continue while waiting for slow operations.
setTimeout schedules a callback to run after the current code finishes.
Async patterns keep the UI responsive during network requests and file I/O.
lessons.challenge: Simulate a slow operation with setTimeout and show how the page remains responsive during the wait.

lessons.title: CPU-Bound vs I/O-Bound Operations
lessons.description: Understand the difference between operations that use the processor and those that wait for external resources.

sections.heading: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound
list: CPU-bound — the processor is busy calculating (math, image processing, loops)
I/O-bound — the program waits for external resources (network, disk, database)
JavaScript handles I/O-bound tasks asynchronously with the event loop
CPU-bound tasks still block the main thread — use Web Workers for heavy computation

codeExamples.heading: CPU-bound blocking example
explanation: The loop blocks the thread — the page is unresponsive until it completes.
The fetch is I/O-bound — the thread continues while the network request happens.
I/O operations use the event loop to stay non-blocking.
For heavy CPU work, use Web Workers to offload to a separate thread.

practice.task: Write a for loop that takes about 2 seconds and observe the page freezing. Then replace it with a setTimeout that simulates the same delay without blocking.
hints: Use a large loop count: for (let i = 0; i < 1e9; i++) {}.
Observe the page becomes unresponsive during the loop.
Replace with setTimeout(() => { ... }, 2000) — the page stays responsive.

keyTakeaways: CPU-bound operations block the main thread — keep them short or offload to Web Workers.
I/O-bound operations are handled asynchronously by the event loop.
JavaScript excels at I/O-bound tasks — network requests, file reads, database queries.
The event loop coordinates between your code and the browser's background tasks.
lessons.challenge: Explain why a web page can handle thousands of concurrent network requests but freezes on a simple 10-million iteration loop.

lessons.title: Basic Async Timers: setTimeout & setInterval
lessons.description: Schedule code to run later with setTimeout and repeat with setInterval.

sections.heading: Timer basics
list: setTimeout(fn, ms) — runs fn after ms milliseconds, once
setInterval(fn, ms) — runs fn every ms milliseconds
Both return an ID you can use with clearTimeout(id) or clearInterval(id)
The delay is a minimum — the actual time may be longer if the thread is busy

codeExamples.heading: setTimeout and setInterval
explanation: setTimeout runs the callback once after the delay.
setInterval repeats the callback at the specified interval.
Always store the ID to clear the timer when needed.
The delay is a minimum — the callback won't run if the thread is blocked.

practice.task: Create a countdown timer that logs 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, "Go!" using setInterval, then stops.
hints: Decrement count each tick and clear the interval when count reaches 0.

keyTakeaways: setTimeout runs code once after a delay; setInterval repeats.
Both are non-blocking — the rest of your code runs immediately.
The delay is a minimum — actual timing depends on the event loop queue.
lessons.challenge: Build a stopwatch with start, stop and reset using setInterval. Display elapsed seconds on the page.
